chunks.text: Existing Multimodal Medical Datasets Medical multimodal datasets have evolved from report-paired corpora such as MIMIC-CXR-JPG ( Johnson et al., 2019 ) to large image-caption collections like PMC-OA ( Lin et al., 2023 ) , case/VQA resources (PMC-CaseReport, PMC-VQA) ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) , instruction-style sets from PubMed imagery (LLaVA-Med VQA, PubMedVision) ( Li et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024b ) , structured annotation efforts (RadGenome-Chest CT) ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , and multigranular pipelines such as MedTrinity ( Xie et al., 2024 ) , Hulu-Med Data ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) , Lingshu Data ( Xu et al., 2025 ) and HealthGPT Data ( Lin et al., 2025 ) . Despite this progress, much of the available supervision remains image-level: a displayed image is paired with a caption, a short answer, or a generated instruction. This creates workflow-sparse supervision because intermediate diagnostic fields and evidence provenance are not consistently represented. It also creates case-fragmented supervision because views, slices, sequences, and non-imaging signals from the same clinical study are often separated into independent examples. Recent resources that include multi-view inputs or richer clinical context, such as MedThinkVQA ( Yao et al., 2025 ) and MedXpertQA ( Zuo et al., 2025 ) , are valuable for evaluation but remain too small to train large medical MLLMs at scale. MultiViewDx differs by organizing training data around evidence-linked clinical cases: it aligns multi-view studies with patient context, normalizes reports into staged diagnostic fields, and constrains instruction synthesis with retrieved source evidence. Medical Multimodal Models Several efforts fine-tune general-purpose multimodal models on medical data and show strong gains.

Med-Flamingo ( Moor et al., 2023 ) adapts OpenFlamingo-9B ( Chen et al., 2024a ) with a medical corpus, and Med-PaLM ( Tu et al., 2024 ) extends PaLM-E ( Driess et al., 2023 ) using large-scale medical image-text pairs. Similarly, LLaVA-Med, Med-Gemini ( Saab et al., 2024 ) , HuatuoGPT-Vision ( Chen et al., 2024b ) , HealthGPT ( Lin et al., 2025 ) , Lingshu ( Xu et al., 2025 ) and Hulu-Med ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) leverage instruction tuning over curated PubMed-derived image-text data for medical QA. Our focus is complementary to model-architecture work. We do not propose a new fusion module; instead, we study how changing the supervision unit from isolated images to evidence-linked clinical cases affects both held-out MedVQA performance and case-based diagnostic reasoning. 4 Training and Evaluation Pipeline This section defines how MultiViewDx is used for training and evaluation. We first describe the three training stages and the controlled variants used in ablations. We then define the benchmark splits, baseline groups, and diagnostic-reasoning metrics. All results are reported in Sec. 5 . 4.1 Training Pipeline We train MultiViewDx-8B in three stages. Stage 1 performs medical image-text pretraining on 14M filtered PMC samples after removing corrupted items, non-medical examples, and captions with fewer than 20 words. Only the adapter is updated, using learning rate 1 ​ e − 4 1\mathrm{e}{-4} , image token length 512, DeepSpeed Stage 2, batch size 8, gradient accumulation 6, and 4 H100 GPUs for 420 hours. Stage 2 performs instruction tuning on GPT-4o-synthesized MultiViewDx instructions, updating all parameters with learning rate 2 ​ e − 5 2\mathrm{e}{-5} , DeepSpeed Stage 2, batch size 6, gradient accumulation 6, and 8 H100 GPUs for 80 hours. Stage 3 sequentially fine-tunes the model on human-annotated clinical cases with learning rate 1 ​ e − 5 1\mathrm{e}{-5} .

The full pipeline uses approximately 2,400 H100 GPU-hours and an estimated 0.81 0.81 – 1.0 × 10 21 1.0\times 10^{21} FLOPs. Multi-image representation. MultiViewDx-8B is initialized from an LLaVA-8B model. Each image is independently encoded by the shared vision encoder and represented as a block of 512 visual tokens. For a multi-image case, visual blocks are serialized in case order with available modality, view, or slice identifiers in the accompanying text; standard one-dimensional sequence positions continue across the serialized visual and textual input. CT and MRI use the selected 2D slices described in Sec. 3.1 , ordered by slice position when available. Training variants. We use six variants to isolate the data and training components. • MultiViewDx-8B-20M uses all available slices from 3D studies during training, and tests whether more visual context alone improves performance. • MultiViewDx-8B-Synthesis uses Stage 1 PMC image-text pretraining followed by GPT-4o-synthesized instruction tuning with the slice-capped case construction and stops before the human-annotated Stage 3. • MultiViewDx-8B-Mix combines GPT-4o-synthesized instructions and human-annotated clinical cases in a single SFT stage. • MultiViewDx-8B-AN first trains on synthesized instructions and then sequentially fine-tunes on human-annotated clinical cases. • MultiViewDx-Non-Multi-View keeps diagnostic-reasoning targets and human-annotated cases, but breaks case-level multi-view grouping into single-view or independently sampled examples. • MultiViewDx-NoReasoning keeps case-level inputs and human-annotated data, but reduces target outputs to direct answers or diagnoses without the evidence-linked diagnostic trajectory. The last two variants test case-fragmented supervision and workflow-sparse supervision. The Non-Multi-View ablation jointly changes case organization and the associated training distribution.

Appendix B.8 illustrates the evidence-linking contrast through paired same-case outputs and reports an inference-time view-removal test. 4.2 Evaluation Pipeline Training and evaluation splits. For VQA-RAD, SLAKE, PathVQA, and PMC-VQA, we follow the official dataset partitions. Only official training splits are used during fine-tuning, and all reported results use the corresponding official held-out test splits. For the JAMA Clinical Challenge, we construct a disjoint case-level split because the dataset does not provide the same predefined train/test split as the VQA benchmarks: 60% of cases are used for training and 40% are reserved for testing. No held-out MedVQA test instance or held-out JAMA case is used during training. MultiViewDx-8B-AN uses all four official benchmark training partitions. PMC-VQA ∗ shares PMC/PMC-OA source provenance with the Stage 1 corpus. Evaluation axes. We evaluate two axes. The first is target-supervised performance on official held-out MedVQA test splits, measured by accuracy on VQA-RAD Lau et al. (2018) , SLAKE Liu et al. (2021) , PathVQA He et al. (2020) , and PMC-VQA Zhang et al. (2023) . The second is case-based diagnostic reasoning, measured on held-out JAMA Clinical Challenge cases that require integration of case context and imaging evidence. For existing MedVQA benchmarks, we report answer accuracy on the official held-out test sets. For JAMA, we report close-ended accuracy when applicable, UMLS-F1 factuality, GPT-4o rubric scores, and clinician ratings. UMLS-F1 measures medical concept overlap using SciSpacy/UMLS, as described in Appendix A.2 . The GPT-4o rubric is a blinded 0–2 scoring protocol designed with clinicians.

It contains three axes: Key Points , which measures coverage of critical clinical elements; Inference , which measures the correctness and completeness of the diagnostic reasoning path; and Evidence , which measures whether claims are grounded in specific findings, imaging views or ROIs, and clinical signals. Overall is the mean of the three rubric axes. To reduce stylistic bias, outputs are style-normalized before judging, and the judge sees extracted gold summaries of Key Points, Inference, and Evidence rather than the full reference text. We also conduct a separate clinician evaluation on 100 randomly sampled held-out JAMA cases. Three clinicians review each case and its gold rationale and assign one holistic rating to the model rationale while considering Key Points, Inference, and Evidence. The averaged and normalized rating is Doctor Score , our primary human evaluation of model rationales. GPT-4o and DeepSeek provide complementary automatic scores; all three evaluations rank MultiViewDx-AN first. Knowledge and inference item classification. We estimate the proportion of knowledge-oriented and inference-oriented items using a fixed GPT-4o judging prompt. For each benchmark item, the input to the judge includes the question, answer choices when available, and the reference answer. The judge assigns one of two labels. A question is labeled knowledge if it mainly requires recognition of a visual pattern, recall of a medical fact, or a short image-text association. A question is labeled inference if it requires combining multiple findings, using clinical context, comparing possible diagnoses, reasoning across views or modalities, or making a multi-step clinical judgment. We apply the same prompt to all datasets to characterize the proportion of knowledge-oriented and inference-oriented items, as shown in Appendix Fig. 4 . The full prompt is provided in Appendix B.5 .

These labels are used only for aggregate characterization of benchmark style, not as gold diagnostic labels for model evaluation. 4.2 Evaluation Pipeline Training and evaluation splits. First, does MultiViewDx retain strong performance on existing MedVQA benchmarks? Second, does it improve case-based diagnostic reasoning beyond MedVQA accuracy? Third, which components of the data design and training schedule matter? Fourth, do clinician judgments and qualitative cases support the automatic results? Additional baseline details, training configurations, and prompt templates are provided in Appendix B.1 . 5.1 Performance on Existing MedVQA Benchmarks Table 2 compares MultiViewDx-8B-AN with proprietary models, general-purpose multimodal VLMs, and medical multimodal VLMs on VQA-RAD, SLAKE, PathVQA, and PMC-VQA ∗ . MultiViewDx-8B-AN achieves the best average accuracy among the compared systems, reaching 79.0%. It outperforms the strongest medical baseline Hulu-Med-7B (74.3%) and HuatuoGPT-Vision-34B (66.7%), and also exceeds strong general-purpose models such as Gemini-2.5-Flash (63.8%), GPT-4.1 (62.0%), and Claude3-Opus (55.7%). MultiViewDx-8B-AN is trained on all four official benchmark training partitions and evaluated on the corresponding held-out test sets. Appendix Tables 13 – 14 report model-by-model training exposure. We therefore evaluate on held-out JAMA Clinical Challenge cases, which provide real-world clinical vignettes with case context and associated visual evidence. Table 4 reports close-ended accuracy, UMLS-F1 factuality, GPT-4o rubric scores for Key Points, Inference, and Evidence when available. MultiViewDx-AN achieves the best Accuracy (58.5%), the highest UMLS Factuality (0.23), and the best GPT-4 Overall score ( 1.29 ± 0.02 1.29\pm 0.02 ). It also obtains the highest Key-Points score (1.28), strong Inference (1.32), and high Evidence (1.27). Among baselines, Claude3-Opus achieves the strongest Inference score (1.56) but weaker Evidence (0.67), while Huatuo-34B provides the strongest Evidence score among baselines (1.31) but lower Inference (1.06). Hulu-Med-7B and Lingshu-7B obtain relatively strong overall rubric scores ( 1.22 ± 0.03 1.22\pm 0.03 and 1.18 ± 0.04 1.18\pm 0.04 ), suggesting that medical-domain training improves evidence-oriented outputs, but still does not fully match MultiViewDx-AN on overall case-based diagnostic reasoning. Fig. 4 further shows that JAMA contains a larger share of inference-oriented items than existing MedVQA benchmarks. Traditional VQA sets are dominated by knowledge items (SLAKE 78.1%, VQA-RAD 76.4%, PathVQA 69.2%), so models can score well by recalling single-view facts or template associations; JAMA contains far fewer knowledge items (44.9%) and instead requires inference from multiple views/modalities (Fig. 4 ). This mismatch explains why surface accuracy on VQA can overstate clinical readiness: those tests rarely require cross-view corroboration, ROI grounding, or contradiction checks. Case-level supervision supports triangulation across views, disambiguation through view-dependent cues, evidence attribution to specific views or ROIs, and study-level coherence. All values reported here match Table 4 ; Appendix Table 7 provides the DeepSeek sensitivity analysis. On 100 multi-view cases, removing the view containing the relevant image evidence while retaining the vignette and remaining inputs reduced accuracy to 31%. The result shows that view-specific evidence is essential during inference.

We use the variants defined in Sec. 4.1 to test which parts of MultiViewDx matter. The ablations are designed to answer four questions. First, does a compact slice-capped case representation work better than feeding all available 3D slices? Second, is sequential fine-tuning on human-annotated clinical cases more effective than mixing synthetic and human cases in one SFT stage? Third, does case-level multi-view organization matter after controlling for reasoning supervision and human cases? Fourth, does explicit evidence-linked reasoning supervision matter after controlling for multi-view inputs and human cases? Training schedule ablation. Table 5 shows the effect of slice selection and training schedule on standard medical VQA benchmarks. MultiViewDx-8B-20M, which uses all available slices from 3D studies, obtains 63.8 average accuracy. Using slice-capped GPT-4o-synthesized instruction data improves the average score to 67.1, suggesting that densely adjacent slices do not necessarily help when they introduce redundant visual context. Mixing synthesized data with human-annotated clinical cases further improves the score to 72.2.

The best result is obtained by MultiViewDx-8B-AN, which first trains on synthesized instruction data and then sequentially fine-tunes on human-annotated cases, reaching 79.0 average accuracy. This suggests that human-annotated cases are most effective when used as a later expert-case alignment stage rather than simply mixed into one SFT stage. Component-level clinician evaluation. Table 6 complements the automatic VQA ablation with clinician evaluation on JAMA. MultiViewDx-Synthesis uses synthetic instruction data and diagnosis-reasoning supervision but does not include case-level multi-view grouping or human-annotated case fine-tuning, obtaining a Doctor Score of 0.30. MultiViewDx-Non-Multi-View adds human-annotated cases but removes case-level multi-view organization, yielding a Doctor Score of 0.29. MultiViewDx-NoReasoning keeps multi-view inputs and human-annotated cases but removes explicit diagnosis-reasoning supervision, leading to the lowest Doctor Score of 0.11. MultiViewDx-AN includes all components and obtains the highest Doctor Score of 0.53. The NoMV–AN gap shows the value of case-level organization under the associated training distribution. MultiViewDx-AN obtains the highest Doctor Score (0.53), above Hulu-Med-7B (0.50) and Claude3-Opus (0.48). The margin is modest, so we interpret it together with the ablations and qualitative cases rather than treating the score alone as sufficient evidence. The qualitative JAMA case in Appendix Table 10 illustrates the same pattern. Appendix Table 11 additionally contrasts illustrative Full and Non-Multi-View outputs on the same case. The case requires linking bilateral optic nerve edema and macular edema with pregnancy, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease, then prioritizing blood pressure assessment to rule out malignant hypertension. MultiViewDx connects the visual findings with the patient context and explains why vital-sign assessment is the immediate next step. Claude3-Opus selects the correct action but gives a less evidence-specific rationale, while HuatuoGPT-Vision variants focus on diabetes-related testing and miss the urgent prioritization. The example suggests that MultiViewDx’s advantage lies in evidence grounding and clinical prioritization, not only in final answer selection. 5.5 Interpretation The results support the two data-design claims in different ways. MedVQA gains show that workflow-aware, report-anchored supervision improves medical image QA performance on held-out test sets.

The JAMA results and ablations provide the stronger test of diagnostic reasoning: removing case-level multi-view grouping weakens performance even when reasoning supervision and human cases remain, and removing evidence-linked reasoning targets causes the largest drop in clinician-rated quality. Thus, the main effect is not explained by parameter scale or by adding more images alone; it comes from organizing supervision around evidence-linked clinical cases. 5.3 Ablations: Workflow, Case Organization, and Training Schedule Variant VQA-RAD SLAKE PathVQA PMC-VQA ∗ Avg. MultiViewDx-AN obtains the highest Doctor Score (0.53), above Hulu-Med-7B (0.50) and Claude3-Opus (0.48). The margin is modest, so we interpret it together with the ablations and qualitative cases rather than treating the score alone as sufficient evidence. The qualitative JAMA case in Appendix Table 10 illustrates the same pattern. Appendix Table 11 additionally contrasts illustrative Full and Non-Multi-View outputs on the same case. The case requires linking bilateral optic nerve edema and macular edema with pregnancy, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease, then prioritizing blood pressure assessment to rule out malignant hypertension. MultiViewDx connects the visual findings with the patient context and explains why vital-sign assessment is the immediate next step. Claude3-Opus selects the correct action but gives a less evidence-specific rationale, while HuatuoGPT-Vision variants focus on diabetes-related testing and miss the urgent prioritization. The example suggests that MultiViewDx’s advantage lies in evidence grounding and clinical prioritization, not only in final answer selection. 6 Limitations and Ethical Considerations MultiViewDx has several limitations. First, modality and anatomy coverage remain uneven because high-quality human-validated clinical data are scarce. Performance may therefore vary across body regions, acquisition protocols, institutions, and patient populations that are underrepresented in the corpus. Second, our representation of 3D CT and MRI studies uses selected 2D slices rather than full volumetric reasoning. The slice-capped strategy is practical and empirically useful in our experiments, but it does not replace architectures designed for full 3D fusion. Third, part of the corpus is retrieval-synthesized. Although physician review finds a low rate of incorrect or misleading reasoning in the sampled cases, this does not eliminate all unsupported statements or subtle evidence-attribution errors.

Fourth, clinician evaluation is conducted on a finite sample of held-out JAMA cases and should be expanded across specialties and institutions. Current validation includes a random, unstratified physician audit of 100 synthesized cases. Future audits will stratify by source, modality, diagnosis, and synthesis workflow. PMC-VQA and Stage 1 share PMC/PMC-OA provenance, and the retained PMC manifests provide sample-level counts rather than unique patient-, study-, or case-level counts. Future validation will quantify retrieval relevance and atomic claim entailment, clinically review the 300,000-instance Chinese subset, and calibrate automatic rubric scores against clinician ratings on matched outputs. The dataset and model are intended for research on medical multimodal reasoning, not for autonomous diagnosis. Any clinical use would require prospective validation, institution-specific calibration, uncertainty reporting, bias and subgroup analysis, and human oversight. We also avoid using identifiable patient information and preserve only de-identified clinical context, but de-identification and data governance should be re-audited before any redistribution or deployment. 7 Conclusion We identify two data limitations that make medical MLLMs appear stronger on MedVQA than on diagnosis-oriented cases: workflow-sparse supervision and case-fragmented supervision. MultiViewDx addresses these limitations by using evidence-linked clinical cases as the training unit, aligning multi-view imaging evidence with patient context and staged diagnostic fields. Fine-tuning on MultiViewDx improves performance on existing MedVQA held-out test sets and yields stronger performance on held-out JAMA case-based diagnostic reasoning. Controlled ablations and clinician evaluation further show that the gains depend on both case-level multi-view organization and explicit evidence-linked reasoning targets.

A.2 UMLS-F1 Factuality Metric To evaluate the factual accuracy of LLM outputs, we leverage the UMLS concept overlap metric. The Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) Bodenreider (2004) enhances biomedical interoperability by unifying a comprehensive collection of biomedical terminologies, classification systems, and coding standards. By reconciling semantic variances and representational disparities across different biomedical repositories, UMLS facilitates standardized understanding. We employ the Scispacy library 2 2 2 Using the Scispacy en_core_sci_lg model to identify and align medical named entities in texts with their corresponding UMLS concepts. Scispacy excels in entity recognition, enabling accurate association of named entities in LLM outputs with relevant UMLS concepts, a critical capability for assessing factual accuracy. Our analytical process utilizes precision and recall metrics. Precision measures the proportion of shared concepts between the LLM output and the ground truth, indicating factual correctness. Recall assesses how well the LLM output covers the concepts present in the ground truth, reflecting the relevance of the information. Formally, given the concept sets from the ground truth ( C ref C_{\text{ref}} ) and the LLM output ( C gen C_{\text{gen}} ), precision and recall are calculated as: Precision = | C ref ∩ C gen | | C gen | , \text{Precision}=\frac{|C_{\text{ref}}\cap C_{\text{gen}}|}{|C_{\text{gen}}|}, (1) Recall = | C ref ∩ C gen | | C ref | .

\text{Recall}=\frac{|C_{\text{ref}}\cap C_{\text{gen}}|}{|C_{\text{ref}}|}. (2) The F1 score, derived from these precision and recall values, provides a balanced measure of the LLM output’s accuracy and relevance. Model Acc. B.5 Prompt for Knowledge/Inference Classification We use GPT-4o to classify each benchmark item as knowledge-oriented or inference-oriented. You are classifying medical QA examples into two categories. Input: Question: [QUESTION] Answer choices: [CHOICES, if available] Reference answer: [REFERENCE ANSWER] Label the example as one of the following: Knowledge: the question can be answered mainly by recognizing a visual pattern, recalling a medical fact, or matching a short image-text association. It does not require combining multiple evidence sources or multi-step clinical reasoning.

Inference: the question requires combining multiple findings, using clinical context, comparing differential diagnoses, reasoning across views or modalities, or making a multi-step clinical judgment. Return only one label: Knowledge or Inference. B.6 Template Prompt Generate Instruction Data. We construct instruction data with both closed-ended and open-ended formats. For close-ended datasets (e.g., PMC-VQA, AMBOSS, JAMA train, SLAKE train, VQA-RAD train, PathVQA), we generate only answer options. For open-ended tasks (mainly from JAMA), we additionally require step-by-step reasoning. We use GPT-4o to generate question-answer pairs from each image and its augmented caption (3-10 QAPs per caption), and we constrain generation to be grounded in the provided caption and image evidence (including ROI-level cues when available). Full prompt templates are shown in Github. Evaluation Pipeline Prompt. For close-ended QA we report accuracy. For open-ended diagnostic reasoning, we use two stricter metrics: UMLS-based factuality and a GPT-4o rubric along Key Points , Inference , and Evidence . To reduce style bias, we first normalize model outputs into a consistent style, then ask the judge to score each aspect independently based on extracted summaries. Prompt details are provided in our Github. B.7 JAMA Case Study: Clinical Prioritization Table 10 presents a qualitative JAMA case study used to analyze diagnostic reasoning behavior across models. The case requires more than recognizing ophthalmic image findings: the model must combine bilateral optic nerve edema, pregnancy, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease to prioritize immediate vital-sign assessment for possible malignant hypertension.

This example supports the main-paper discussion that clinical diagnostic reasoning is not fully captured by answer accuracy alone and that models may fail by over-weighting a salient but less urgent disease prior, such as diabetes, instead of selecting the clinically urgent next step. Table 10: JAMA case study illustrating a clinical prioritization error. Clinical Prioritization Error Question. A woman in her mid-20s presented with subacute bilateral vision loss that was worse in the left eye. Her medical history was remarkable for type 1 diabetes diagnosed at 16 years of age and proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes that had been treated with panretinal photocoagulation 7 years earlier. She had undergone pars plana vitrectomy with endolaser to treat a tractional retinal detachment in her right eye 2 years before this presentation. She also had a history of hypertension and chronic kidney disease, and she was 15 weeks into pregnancy. Visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/100 OS. Intraocular pressure was normal bilaterally, and no relative afferent pupillary defect was detected. Findings of an anterior segment examination were normal. The patient was in no apparent distress and denied any headache, chest pain, or focal weakness. Ophthalmoscopic examination (Figure) revealed mild optic nerve head edema that was greater in the left eye than the right eye with associated nerve fiber layer hemorrhage in the left eye. Nerve fiber layer infarctions, dot and blot hemorrhages, and lesions caused by panretinal photocoagulation also were seen bilaterally. Optical coherence tomography showed macular edema that involved the center of the macula in both eyes (Figure, inset). Choices: (A) Obtain a fluorescein angiogram; (B) Determine blood glucose level and perform glycated hemoglobin test; (C) Measure heart rate, respiratory rate, and blood pressure; (D) Perform immediate computed tomography of the head.

Correct Answer: (C) Measure heart rate, respiratory rate, and blood pressure. Clinical Diagnosis: Malignant hypertension with papillopathy. Diagnostic Reason: Malignant hypertension with papillopathy C. Measure heart rate, respiratory rate, and blood pressure The patient was found to have hypertension , with a blood pressure of 195/110 mm Hg . Heart and respiratory rates were normal. Measurement of the arterial blood pressure may be performed rapidly in the clinic with a sphygmomanometer and is essential to rule out malignant hypertension , which is a potentially life-threatening cause of vision loss . Although the differential diagnosis for bilateral optic nerve edema is broad, workup should always include assessment of blood pressure when appropriate, because a hypertensive emergency (also known as malignant hypertension ) may cause substantial morbidity or mortality if not diagnosed and treated promptly. Findings may include macular star , macular edema , serous retinal detachment , intraretinal hemorrhage , and optic disc edema with or without associated hemorrhage 1,2 . Optic nerve head edema may occur with systolic blood pressures as low as 160 mm Hg , with the median onset occurring at 188 mm Hg . 3 The macular edema associated with hypertensive retinopathy may be distributed more nasally, as was seen in this patient. 4 This patient had mild optic nerve edema despite high systemic blood pressure and substantial macular edema. This less-pronounced optic nerve edema likely was attributable to optic nerve atrophy at baseline. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy and panretinal photocoagulation can be associated with optic atrophy, and atrophic optic nerves tend to become less edematous than healthy optic nerves. 5-7 .

Regarding the other choices above, a fluorescein angiogram (choice A) would be expected to show leakage from the optic nerve and macula, but such findings are already available from the optical coherence tomography , which showed intraretinal and subretinal fluid . Although assessment of serologic levels of glucose and glycated hemoglobin (choice B) is important in the management of diabetic retinopathy, results from such tests are not immediately available and have less bearing on the immediate management of the case (this patient’s glycated hemoglobin level was 10.5% [to convert to a proportion of total hemoglobin, multiply by 0.01]). Performing computed tomography (choice D) would be a reasonable later step, especially if the patient’s blood pressure was found to be normal, to rule out an intracranial mass . In addition to hypertension, other causes of optic nerve head edema exist. Papilledema (when optic nerve head edema is secondary to increased intracranial pressure ) is often bilateral and may be caused by intracranial mass lesions , meningitis , cerebral venous thrombosis , or intracranial hypertension , or it may be idiopathic. Bilateral optic nerve head edema also may be caused by diabetic papillopathy (which is a rare cause of optic disc edema, but which is bilateral in up to 50% of cases 8,9 ) and toxic optic neuropathies . Optic disc drusen are frequently bilateral and may cause so-called pseudopapilledema . 10 Severe hypertension resulting in acute retinopathy and optic nerve head edema is considered a hypertensive emergency because of its association with end-organ damage , namely, damage to the retina and optic nerve .

This case serves as a reminder that, although the differential diagnosis for optic nerve head edema is broad, immediately assessing the patient’s blood pressure to evaluate for hypertensive emergency in the eye clinic may be critical , because this treatable condition could lead to substantial morbidity or mortality if diagnosis is delayed. The patient was admitted to the medicine service for management of hypertension . At an ophthalmology follow-up examination 3 months later, her blood pressure was 128/73 mm Hg and her visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/60 OS , close to her visual acuity before this acute event. On examination, the optic nerve head edema had resolved , and optical coherence tomography showed resolution of macular edema . Prediction Rationale MultiViewDx. C.
